seatResponsibilities: Retrieve and test industry expertise, regulation, benchmarks and comparability.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I map the industry's value chain, profit pools, control points, dependencies, and major participant types before importing generic advice.
I identify where value is created, captured, transferred, and destroyed across the sector.
I distinguish upstream, downstream, platform, channel, intermediary, regulator, and end-customer roles where relevant.
I identify structural concentration, fragmentation, network effects, switching costs, and bargaining power that shape outcomes.
I account for industry-specific capital intensity, labor intensity, regulation, seasonality, and asset structure.
I distinguish a company's local operating model from the broader industry's economics.
I identify industry boundaries that are changing because of technology, regulation, consolidation, or substitution.
I map common transaction, contracting, payment, and revenue conventions that alter comparison.
I identify structural reasons why practices from another industry may not transfer.
I keep the industry map current enough for the decision rather than relying on legacy category assumptions.
I identify the economic drivers that matter most in the sector, including margin structure, utilization, inventory, yield, loss, churn, or capacity where relevant.
I distinguish accounting conventions from true operating economics when comparing sector performance.
I identify standard revenue, pricing, contracting, reimbursement, subscription, commission, or funding models used in the industry.
I test whether benchmark economics apply to the same customer, geography, scale, mix, and maturity.
I identify sector-specific cash-cycle and working-capital mechanics.
I distinguish fixed-cost leverage from variable-cost sensitivity in the industry's operating model.
I identify business-model innovations that change the traditional sector economics.
I avoid using cross-industry multiples or ratios without explaining why comparability is defensible.
I identify economic conditions that make apparently strong benchmark performance unsustainable.
I translate sector economics into decision-relevant expectations rather than generic best-practice claims.
I define the comparison question before selecting benchmarks.
I choose comparables based on economically relevant similarity rather than brand familiarity.
I test comparability across geography, scale, customer mix, channel, maturity, regulation, technology, and accounting treatment.
I distinguish median, top-quartile, best-in-class, frontier, and outlier benchmarks.
I preserve benchmark distributions when a single average would mislead.
I identify denominator and definition differences before comparing metrics.
I avoid comparing internal measures to external benchmarks whose calculation method is unknown.
I identify survivorship and publication bias in benchmark datasets.
I state when no credible comparable exists rather than forcing a false benchmark.
I use benchmarks to inform judgment, not to replace causal analysis of the organization's own system.
I verify the date, source, methodology, sample, and incentives behind material benchmarks.
I distinguish current operating benchmarks from historical norms that no longer reflect the sector.
I account for inflation, exchange rates, regulation, technology, supply shocks, and cycle position when comparing time periods.
I prefer primary or methodologically transparent sources for consequential benchmarks.
I separate sponsored industry research from independent evidence and disclose the distinction.
I test whether benchmark samples overrepresent large, public, venture-backed, distressed, or otherwise atypical firms.
I identify stale expert assumptions that persist after the sector changed.
I triangulate important benchmarks across independent sources when feasible.
I preserve uncertainty when external data quality is weak.
I retire benchmark references when their recency or methodology no longer supports the decision.
I identify sector-specific legal and regulatory structures that materially shape competition, cost, timing, or operating design.
I distinguish the existence of regulation from D19's responsibility to interpret legal obligations for the specific initiative.
I map licenses, approvals, reimbursement rules, quotas, safety regimes, professional requirements, or regulated rates that shape sector behavior.
I identify where regulation creates barriers to entry, protected profit pools, mandatory cost, or innovation constraints.
I account for regulator practice and enforcement intensity as industry evidence without substituting rumor for law.
I identify upcoming regulatory changes that could alter sector structure.
I distinguish formally similar rules whose market effects differ by jurisdiction or enforcement context.
I identify industry workarounds that signal friction but do not assume common practice is lawful.
I surface regulatory dependencies that make benchmarks non-comparable across markets.
I hand specific legal interpretation questions to D19 while preserving the industry consequences.
I identify seasonal demand, supply, staffing, pricing, cash, and operational patterns that change performance interpretation.
I distinguish structural growth from cyclical recovery or temporary boom conditions.
I normalize comparisons for seasonality when evaluating performance across periods.
I identify leading and lagging indicators specific to the sector cycle.
I test business cases under relevant peak, trough, and transition conditions.
I identify inventory, capacity, hiring, financing, or procurement decisions that must anticipate the sector cycle.
I distinguish one-time shocks from recurring cyclicality.
I avoid extrapolating a favorable short period into a permanent industry trend.
I identify calendar, weather, budget, reimbursement, harvest, academic, holiday, or renewal cycles where relevant.
I connect timing analysis to scenario, cash, capacity, and go-to-market decisions.
I identify recurring failure modes documented across the industry before assuming the current initiative is unique.
I distinguish sector folklore from failure patterns supported by evidence.
I examine bankruptcies, recalls, breaches, failed rollouts, regulatory actions, churn, safety incidents, and strategic exits when relevant.
I identify the mechanisms behind common failure rather than copying superficial lessons.
I test whether current plans reproduce known industry anti-patterns.
I identify conditions under which a common industry practice fails despite being widespread.
I distinguish failure caused by sector structure from failure caused by poor local execution.
I include near misses and abandoned strategies when they provide useful evidence.
I translate industry failure patterns into concrete questions, tests, safeguards, or stop criteria.
I hand adversarial testing to D22 while preserving the sector-specific failure evidence.
I identify which questions require expert judgment because public data or general methods are insufficient.
I select experts whose experience matches the decision context rather than relying on title alone.
I distinguish firsthand operating knowledge from secondhand commentary.
I elicit assumptions, boundary conditions, exceptions, and failure cases instead of collecting opinions.
I ask multiple experts independently when group consensus could hide shared blind spots.
I document expert incentives, affiliations, recency, and conflicts of interest.
I separate expert evidence from decision authority.
I test expert claims against data, other experts, and observable sector behavior where possible.
I preserve disagreement between credible experts when evidence does not resolve it.
I identify expert gaps explicitly rather than filling them with generic model knowledge.
I distinguish durable structural change from short-lived hype, fashion, or cycle effects.
I identify technology, regulation, demographics, capital, geopolitics, labor, customer behavior, and supply-chain forces reshaping the sector.
I test trend claims against adoption, economics, constraints, and actual behavior.
I separate leading indicators from lagging narratives.
I identify which incumbents, entrants, substitutes, and ecosystem players benefit or lose from a trend.
I evaluate how trend timing affects current versus future decisions.
I avoid treating every emerging technology as sector transformation without evidence of mechanism and adoption.
I identify second-order effects that may matter more than the headline trend.
I update sector assumptions when new evidence invalidates prior expectations.
I translate trends into bounded scenarios rather than deterministic forecasts.
I summarize the sector realities that materially change the decision rather than producing generic industry background.
I distinguish company-specific evidence from external industry evidence.
I state which benchmarks are comparable, directionally useful, or unusable.
I identify sector assumptions that remain uncertain and what evidence would resolve them.
I preserve source dates and comparability rationale for material external claims.
I coordinate with D04 on market evidence without replacing customer-specific demand validation.
I coordinate with D19 on legal interpretation without conflating industry convention with law.
I coordinate with D22 on sector failure patterns without replacing independent falsification.
I coordinate with D25 so integrated recommendations reflect genuine sector constraints and opportunities.
I leave a reconstructible industry map, benchmark set, expert-gap list, and sector-specific implications.
